Once upon a time, computers had only a single core, with a single physical thread, and therefore, they could only run a single operation sequentially.

Nowadays, computers have multiple cores (physical or not), and each can have as many threads as the manufacturer wants, but usually, it goes up to 8, while 2 is very common in intel and AMD processors.

Therefore, it is useful to take advantage of the power that machines have, and running a single program in parallel.

> "Parallel programming can be defined as a model aims to create compatible programs with ready environments to execute code simultaneously." Jan Palach - Parallel Programming with Python

In order to run a program in parallel, we can think of different ways of doing it:

-   Multithreads
-   Multiprocessing
-   Concurrence
-   Async I/O

In order to use one of these methods, we need to firstly understand the problem we need to solve to find the right tool.

## Multithreads

A multithread program is a program that can use multiple threads to run the tasks that needs to be solved. So, the thread itself runs your program. A characteristics of the multiple threads, it is that they all share the same memory and same process and are managed by the OS. A downside of using multithreads it is that only a single thread can execute the code, while all others needs to wait the lock to get relased. It occurs because Python has GIL (Global Interpreter Lock), that allows only a single thread to be executed inside a process at time. In most recent versions, there is a possibility to release this restrain, but you can face more race conditions.

Therefore, in the usual scenario, multiple threads run concurrently: only one can execute, while all others need to wait.

The advantage of using a multithreaded code, it is that if we are facing an Input/Output (I/O) operation (an operation, for example, that needs to wait the server to respond), the threads can operate in the interleave mode.For example: + Thread 1 makes a request in the server and waits the response (The OS places a lock on this thread and picks the second one). + Thread 2 makes the request in the server and waits the response (This thread receives lock). + Thread 1 collects the data from server and finishes. + Thread 2 collects the data from server and finishes.

Even though the threads are not running at the same time, that is the impression for the user because the changes between the threads may occurs in milliseconds.

Threads basically are workers generated within your program that perform tasks inside a single core. If you have more than one thread, you have multithreading. Having a `queue` and the `event` setup, you can generate your pool of `threads`, choosing as many as you want, and they will complete the task for you; finally, you have to send the `kill` "method", so the thread dies at the end and frees memory.

## Multiprocessing

When we run a program in multiprocess, it means that we start the program from a parent process (`os.getppid()`), and from it, multiple processes starts. This multiple child processes runs independently (not concurrently), in parallel (at the same time) because they are GIL free (because are the different process), they do not share the same memory.

This is usefull when you have a CPU operation and you can take usage of as many cores you have on your machine. Even though you can start a multiprocessing code in a single core, the usefulness of this technique is achieved when you allocate each process in a different CPU core.

For simple and light weight operations (I/O), it may take longer than multithreading and it uses more memory, because the objects needs to copied on each process.

A good experiment is to watch how many process are running on you OS.

### Multithreads and Multiprocessing in OS

For example, take a look on `htop` screenshot:

![](htop.png)

We have 198 tasks running, which in this case means processes, and they are using 1526 threads in total, but only 1 is running (all the others 1525 are sleeping, waiting to be called).

So, a OS can start as many processes as it wants (independently of the number of cores), and for each process, having multiple threads associated to id - making it a multithreaded multiprocess operation.

``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
import asyncio


async def fetch(name, delay):  # 1. async def => coroutine function
    print(f"{name} start")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)  # 2. suspend here, let others run
    print(f"{name} done")
    return name


async def main():  # 3. anything that awaits must be async
    results = await asyncio.gather(  # 4. run all three concurrently
        fetch("A", 1),
        fetch("B", 1),
        fetch("C", 1),
    )
    print(results)


asyncio.run(main())  # 5. the ONE sync->async boundary
```
:::

``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="false"}
balance = 100


async def withdraw(amount):
    global balance
    if balance >= amount:  # (1) CHECK
        await asyncio.sleep(0.01)  # (2) SUSPEND — other tasks run here
        balance -= amount  # (3) ACT on a now-stale check


async def main():
    await asyncio.gather(withdraw(100), withdraw(100))
    print(balance)  # -100. Both passed the check before either subtracted.
```
